title: The pandits of Kashmir
hook: Kashmiri Brahmins facing forced conversion come to him for help

segments.voice: Yesterday, journeys east and a new town: Chakk Nanaki, the town that became Anandpur. Your line was build where you are. Did you take one first step? Day seventy-seven.

Look back at this week. A word changed to please a court. A child Guru, calm before the powerful, who served the sick and died in Delhi. A boy renamed brave of the sword, who went quiet at Bakala. A trader shouting from a roof. A new town on rough ground. And now, spring of 1675, at Anandpur. The Guru is home, and his young son, Gobind Rai, is with him. A group of travelers arrives from the far north, from the valley of Kashmir, worn out from the mountain roads. They are pandits, Hindu Brahmin scholars and priests. They are not Sikhs. They've come a long way to ask a Guru for help. Today, the knock at the door.
screen: `A WEEK OF QUIET COURAGE.` → `ANANDPUR, 1675.` → `TRAVELERS FROM KASHMIR.`

segments.voice: Here is what the pandits told the Guru, as Sikh tradition remembers it. Under the emperor Aurangzeb, the Mughal governor of Kashmir was pressing Hindus there to convert to Islam, and the Brahmins, as religious leaders, were under particular pressure. Tradition names their leader Pandit Kirpa Ram, from Mattan, near the town of Anantnag. They had nowhere else to turn. Historians discuss how widespread this policy was, and how the court saw it; the sources are not all agreed. What the Sikh sources agree on is the scene at Anandpur. Three things stand out. First, the pandits were not the Guru's followers. They wore the sacred thread and the forehead mark, practices the Gurus themselves had not taken up. On day six you met Guru Nanak as a boy, refusing to wear it. Second, the Guru's own community was not being threatened in this request. He could have said: this isn't our fight. Third, the Guru listened. Tradition says he sat quietly for a long time, deep in thought, heavy with what they had told him. The question in the air was simple and terrible: who would stand up for the right of other people to practice a faith that wasn't his? Tomorrow and the days after, we'll see his answer, and what it cost. Today, notice only this. The people in need came to him, and he did not send them away.
screen: `PRESSURE TO CONVERT IN KASHMIR.` · `PANDIT KIRPA RAM LEADS THEM.` · `NOT HIS FOLLOWERS, NOT HIS THREAD.` · `THE GURU SITS AND LISTENS.` · then, large: `THEY CAME TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to someone asking for help. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has come to you lately, even in a small way: a message you skimmed, a friend who said I'm fine too quickly, a coworker who needed more than they asked for. Replay it slowly. This time, just listen. Don't plan your answer. Notice what they were really asking. Stay with them, the way the Guru sat with the travelers. The bell holds the time.
The pandits of Kashmir. Hindu scholars under pressure to convert, who traveled to Anandpur in 1675 to ask Guru Tegh Bahadur for help.
Your line: they came to him. Today, when someone comes to you, stop what you're doing and really listen, even for two minutes. Day seventy-seven, the end of another week.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of the Kashmiri pandits coming to Anandpur as the beginning of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, and honor him as one who gave his life for the freedom of others to practice their faith.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Kashmiri pandits, Brahmin scholars of the Kashmir valley.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people asked a holy man for help.
what it means: people of another faith came to a Guru to defend their right to keep it, and he did not send them away.
what a scholar hears: tradition names Pandit Kirpa Ram of Mattan; the same man is later remembered as Kirpa Singh, who took amrit and fell at Chamkaur.
